Follow live updates here. $58 billion in SNAP, SSI and Medicare benefits go unclaimed by older adults — how retirees can save thousands
 Rebecca Payne Mon, October 26, 2026 at 5:00 AM MST 5 min read seventyfourimages/Envato Millions of low-income older adults in America are missing out on benefits that could help them cover costs for medical bills, groceries, utility bills and more. 
 Must Read

 Data from the National Council on Aging (NCOA) show that more than 9 million older adults who are eligible for benefits are not claiming them. 
 Collectively, NCOA says that an estimated $58 billion in benefits that could help to pay for daily essentials are being left on the table. 
 The NCOA says that many older adults may incorrectly believe that they don't qualify for these benefits programs, while others may not even know they exist 
 Thousands in potential help 
 For those low-income older adults who aren't collecting benefits they're eligible for, the dollar amounts being left on the table are significant. 
 The NCOA data looks at three benefit programs: the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), Supplemental Security Income (SSI) and Medicare Savings Programs (MSPs). 
 Just 38% of eligible individuals age 65+ participated in SNAP in 2023, the NCOA found. That means an estimated 9.1 million eligible people didn't claim benefits that could have helped them put food on the table. 
 That's $188 a month, or $2,256 a year, in SNAP benefits that people are missing out on (based on the 2023 average benefit amount for households with a 60+ adult). 
 For SSI, 40% of those eligible participated in 2023, meaning 3.6 million people left those benefits on the table. That amounts to $552.29 a month, or $6,627.48 a year, based on the December 2023 average for adults 65+. 
 And for MSPs, which help cover Medicare premiums, deductibles and co-insurance, 49% of those eligible claimed benefits, meaning 6.6 million people weren't enrolled. That's $164.90 a month unclaimed, or $1,978.80 a year, based on the standard Part B premium for 2023. 
 All told, for someone who qualified for all three benefits programs, based on 2023 benefit levels, that's $10,862.28 a year to help cover life's essentials. 
 There's other help for low-income older adults available as well. Those who qualify for the Medicare Savings Program, and those who receive SSI, also automatically qualify for the Extra Help program , which helps pay for Medicare drug coverage (Part D) and other costs. 
 Story Continues The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) can help with energy bills for low-income individuals. This program is administered at the state level.

 Why are benefits left unclaimed? 
 Older adults may encounter several barriers to applying for benefits programs. 
 Tiara Green, president of nonprofit Accessia Health, told the Washington Post that those in need of assistance programs can face difficulty managing paperwork — different applications and eligibility requirements for different programs, and different government agencies. 
 "The larger problem is that the assistance system is fragmented," Green said. 
 Courtney Bragg, co-founder and CEO of Fabric Health, referred to the array of assistance programs as an "alphabet soup" in the Post's report, and highlighted that older adults are susceptible to fraudsters when it comes to benefits. 
 Bragg noted this can be especially true during open enrollment periods for benefits, flagging the "the predatory environment for seniors." 
 For those older adults seeking assistance, Bragg recommends starting with official government resources, or trusted organizations. 
 Where to get help 
 The NCOA has a benefits search tool you can use to see what programs you could be eligible for. There is also a help line, those who wish to use the telephone (1-800-794-6559). 
 And there is a map of affiliated partners and programs, such as seniors' centers, for those who wish to seek help in person. 
 For help with Medicare, reach out to your State Health Insurance Assistance Program, where you can get free counseling. 
 You can also seek out resources from your local Area Agency on Aging, which you can find using the Eldercare locator. 
 Remember to be vigilant about scammers — government agencies will not charge fees for you to receive a benefit. 
 Many older adults are simply unaware these programs exist, and others incorrectly believe they are ineligible.
